blocks.text:
Design an online chess platform, the system that lets two players play a real-time game of chess against each other, enforcing the actual rules of chess, tracking each player's remaining time on a chess clock, and letting either player reconnect mid-game without losing progress. Unlike this project's highest-throughput designs, a single chess game generates very little traffic, a handful of moves per minute at most, but every one of those moves has to be validated against real chess rules and a real, tamper-resistant clock, entirely on the server, since a client that could claim its own move was legal or report its own elapsed time would make the entire game untrustworthy.

The two techniques that make this trustworthy are server-authoritative move validation, the server, never the client, decides whether a move is legal, and reconstructing a game's current state by replaying its durable move log from the initial position, which is cheap precisely because a real chess game is only ever a few dozen moves long.

blocks.text: Two players should be able to play a game of chess against each other in real time, each move validated against real chess rules before being applied. Each player should have their own chess clock, counting down as they think and gaining a small increment after each move they make. A player whose connection drops should be able to reconnect and resume the game exactly where it left off, with the game itself continuing to exist server-side in the meantime. A game should support spectators who can watch its moves live without being able to affect it.

blocks.text: Five qualities matter here, and the first two are what make a fair, trustworthy game possible at all.
blocks.content: Five qualities matter here, and the first two are what make a fair, trustworthy game possible at all.

blocks.alt: Server-authoritative state, a fair and tamper-proof clock, reconnecting without losing the game, real-time move delivery, and resistance to engine-assisted cheating

blocks.text: Server-authoritative state means the client's own claim about the board is never trusted over the server's own record, every move is validated against the server's authoritative state, not the client's local copy of it. A fair, tamper-proof clock means a player's remaining time is computed from timestamps the server itself observed, never anything the client reports about its own elapsed time. Reconnecting without losing the game means a dropped connection mid-game must never cost either player their progress. Real-time move delivery means an opponent's move should appear within a fraction of a second, not require a manual refresh. And resistance to engine-assisted cheating means a player secretly consulting a chess engine for every move undermines the entire point of playing another human, and needs at least some detection, even if imperfect.

blocks.text: This design assumes matchmaking itself is a separate, lighter-weight concern, pairing two players by rating into a new game session, and focuses instead on the game session itself once it exists. Full legal-move chess rules, including check detection, castling, and en passant, are treated as a deeper layer built on top of the same server-authoritative validation architecture described here, illustrated with a representative movement-rule subset rather than the complete rule set. A player's current game state is assumed reconstructable purely by replaying its own move log from the initial position, since a real chess game's move count is always small enough for this to be cheap.

blocks.text: A large online chess platform might have millions of games in progress concurrently at peak, but any single game generates only a handful of moves per minute, an entirely different load shape from this project's high-throughput designs. Each move fans out to at most two players plus however many spectators happen to be watching that one specific game, a comparatively small, bounded fan-out compared to a viral livestream's comment fan-out. A submitted move is expected to be validated and broadcast to the opponent well under a second after it is made.

blocks.text: Both players connect through a realtime gateway to a dedicated game session service instance that owns their specific game. A submitted move passes through a move validator, checking both turn order and chess-rule legality, and a chess clock deducts the elapsed server-observed time before the move is durably logged and broadcast back through the gateway to the opponent and any spectators. A separate anti-cheat analysis process watches move timing and accuracy patterns across games without sitting on the actual move-validation critical path.

A separate anti-cheat analysis process watches move timing and accuracy patterns across games without sitting on the actual move-validation critical path.

blocks.alt: Both players connect through a realtime gateway to their game's dedicated session service, which validates moves, tracks the chess clock, durably logs every move, and broadcasts to the opponent and spectators, with anti-cheat analysis watching separately

blocks.text: A submitted move is first checked against whose turn it actually is, then against whether it is a legal move for that piece given the current board. Either check failing rejects the move outright, with the turn never actually passing to the opponent for a rejected attempt.
blocks.content: A submitted move is first checked against whose turn it actually is, then against whether it is a legal move for that piece given the current board. Either check failing rejects the move outright, with the turn never actually passing to the opponent for a rejected attempt.

blocks.alt: A submitted move is checked for correct turn order, then chess-rule legality, and only a move passing both checks is applied and passes the turn to the opponent

blocks.text: Rather than persisting a full board snapshot after every move, a game's durable, ordered move log is the true source of truth, and its current state is produced by replaying every move from the initial position. This is cheap specifically because a real chess game is only ever a few dozen moves long, unlike the stock exchange's much higher-volume write-ahead log.

blocks.alt: A game's durable move log is replayed from the initial position to produce its exact current board state, cheap because a typical game is only dozens of moves long

blocks.text: When a move arrives, the server measures how much time has genuinely elapsed since that player's turn began, deducts it from their own remaining time, and only then adds back a small increment. If a player's remaining time reaches zero before their move arrives, they lose immediately on time, regardless of anything the client itself might claim about elapsed time.

blocks.alt: Elapsed time since a player's turn began is measured server-side and deducted from their remaining time; reaching zero ends the game on time, otherwise a small increment is added before the opponent's clock starts

blocks.text: Moves are stored in standard chess notation alongside a strictly increasing move number, making the move log itself both the durability mechanism and a naturally human-readable game history. Because a game's current board state is always fully determined by replaying its move list from the start, no separate mutable board-snapshot table is needed at all, avoiding an entire class of snapshot-versus-log consistency bugs.

blocks.text: The happy path is the move flow above, a legal, on-turn move validated, clocked, and broadcast cleanly. The workflow worth walking through separately is a player reconnecting after a dropped connection, since the game session service itself never stopped owning that game's authoritative state the entire time the player was disconnected, a reconnect is simply a fresh fetch of that same, unchanged state, with the opponent's clock having continued counting down exactly as it would have regardless of the disconnection.

blocks.text: This mirrors the stock exchange design's per-symbol ownership rule, but at the much smaller scale of one game rather than one entire trading symbol, exactly one instance ever owns a given game's authoritative state at a time.

blocks.text: Because each game is small, cheap, and entirely independent of every other game, scaling out is simply a matter of spreading millions of lightweight, independent game sessions across enough hosts, unlike the stock exchange's much heavier per-symbol throughput ceiling.

blocks.text: The move log is partitioned by game id and replicated for durability, since losing a game's history mid-play would be a genuine, disruptive failure for both players. Because any individual game's data is both small and short-lived relative to this project's largest stores, this store scales primarily by spreading enormous game counts across partitions rather than by managing unusually large individual records.

blocks.text: This mirrors the exact same consistency split as the stock exchange and live-comments designs, an authoritative, single-owner sequence for the thing correctness actually depends on, paired with a looser, delay-tolerant view for anyone just watching from the outside.

blocks.alt: A dropped connection leaves a game's durable state and move log completely untouched, and reconnecting simply re-syncs the client to that same, unaffected authoritative state

blocks.text: Because the game session service, not either player's connection, is what actually owns a game's state, a player disconnecting is a routine, fully recoverable event rather than a threat to the game's integrity, exactly the reconnection guarantee both players depend on.

blocks.text: Engine-assisted cheating detection is this design's defining, unique security concern, distinct from every other category's angle in this project, since the threat here is not a manipulated request or a stolen credential, it is a human quietly outsourcing their own decisions to software, undermining the platform's entire premise even when every individual move looks technically legal.

blocks.text: Move validation and broadcast latency is the clearest signal of whether a game session host is keeping up with its assigned games. Anti-cheat flag rates are worth their own dedicated monitoring, both to catch a genuine wave of engine-assisted play and to catch a detector itself producing an unusual number of false positives against ordinary strong human players.

blocks.text: Server-authoritative validation with move-log replay is the right default because it is the only option that makes the game genuinely trustworthy at all, and the replay cost it accepts in exchange is negligible given how short a real chess game actually is.

blocks.text: Keeping a game's state purely as a replayable move log, rather than a separately maintained snapshot, avoids an entire class of extra writes and the reconciliation logic a snapshot-plus-log design would otherwise need. Bounded, per-game spectator fan-out keeps the realtime gateway's cost proportional to genuine audience size rather than a fixed, worst-case allocation for every single game.

blocks.text: A change to move-validation logic needs careful testing against a wide range of real positions, not just simple, common cases, since a subtle bug could let an illegal move through or wrongly reject a legal one, either of which directly breaks trust in the platform. Anti-cheat detection changes deserve particular caution around false positives, wrongly flagging a genuinely strong human player carries a real reputational cost distinct from an ordinary technical bug.

items: Architecture: a dedicated, authoritative game session instance per active game, validating moves and tracking a server-side clock, with a durable move log and bounded fan-out to the opponent and spectators.
Capacity: millions of concurrent games, each generating only a handful of moves per minute, with sub-second move validation and broadcast.
The core techniques: server-authoritative move validation and state reconstruction by replaying a durable move log, both worked through with a real, verified implementation in Java, Python, and C++.
Database: a game-id-partitioned, append-only move log as the single source of truth a game's current state is always reconstructable from.
End-to-end workflows: a normal move flow and a reconnect flow, both traced as sequence diagrams.
Consistency: a strongly consistent, single-authoritative-owner move sequence per game, paired with an eventually consistent spectator view.

Trade-offs: server-authoritative validation with move-log replay versus trusting client-reported moves and timing versus a separately maintained board snapshot, compared directly on trust model and recovery cost.
